member_of.name: Marcus Mumford and his Mary Men (proto-band)

podcast.title: Band Formation and Scouting (2007)
podcast.body: The band was formed in December 2007 and was scouted by Lewis Bloom of Island Records shortly after. Bloom repeatedly saw them perform until he deemed them ready for a record deal. "He scouted Mumford and son, surely after the band was formed in December 2007."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Ben Lovett Leaves Hot Rocket for Mumford & Sons (2007)
podcast.body: In October 2007, despite his band Hot Rocket having a successful indie EP and a sold-out UK tour, Ben Lovett chose to leave Hot Rocket, his record deal, and the tour to join the nascent "foaky thing" that would become Mumford & Sons, feeling a stronger connection to their music. "So he made a decision."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Precursor to Mumford & Sons (2007)
podcast.body: This group, consisting of Marcus, Ted, and Winston, performed at the bar Communion, where Ben Lovett would occasionally join them on stage. By October 2007, they began recording together, which ultimately led to their transformation into Mumford & Sons. "Meanwhile, Marcus, Ted and Winston had coalesced in a group called Marcus Mumford and his Mary Men."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Early Perception at Island Records (2008)
podcast.body: In an early 2008 meeting at Island Records, Mumford & Sons were initially dismissed as an unconventional "banjo band" or "dustbin merchants" whose use of an accordion was seen as highly unorthodox, reflecting a label's skepticism about their potential in the alternative music market. "Next thing you'll tell me is that they have an accordion player."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Appearance and Impact (2009)
podcast.body: This band appeared around 2009, sounding fresh and different. They achieved significant commercial success and had both cross-genre and cross-generational appeal, helping to usher in a new generation of softer and poppier alt rock, and sparking a folk scene growth in Britain. "When they appeared, they sounded fresh and different."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of the 2010s Part 2: The Role of Indie Rock

podcast.title: Debut Album Cover Photo (2009)
podcast.body: The *Sigh No More* album cover, featuring all four band members in the window of Pimpernell & Partners (a 19th-century furniture shop at 596 The Kings Road, London), was shot by Max Knight in Summer 2009. The photograph took nearly eight hours to capture due to challenges such as a very hot day, the band arriving late, a busy street requiring clear shots (no cars, pedestrians, or cats), sun reflections ruining takes, and distractions from drunk Wimbledon watchers in a neighboring pub. "It's all four members of the band in the window of a shop at 596, The Kings Road, and the full area of London."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Marcus Mumford's Crisis of Faith (2009)
podcast.body: During the recording of *Sigh No More* in 2009, Marcus Mumford experienced a "crisis of faith," struggling to reconcile the allure of the "rock and roll world" with his parents' evangelical Christian beliefs. "And to make things even weirder, Marcus was having a crisis of faith."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Self-Financed Debut Album (2009)
podcast.body: For their debut album, the band was required to finance the entire production themselves, an estimated 20,000 pounds, and create their own indie label as part of a deal with Lewis Bloom and Island Records. "The total for everything will be about 20,000 pounds and it will be all your money."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Unique Sound in 2009 Musical Landscape
podcast.body: In 2009, Mumford & Sons' English folk sound, featuring accordions, banjos, and ukuleles, was considered "a million miles away from what anyone else was offering," providing a stark contrast to the dominant alt-rock bands and pop stars like Beyonce, Katy Perry, and Justin Bieber. "What Mumford was offering the world in 2009 was a million miles away from what anyone else was offering."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Comparison to Fairground Attraction
podcast.body: Fairground Attraction is described as "the Mumford and sons of their day," suggesting a similar folk-pop style and level of popularity in their era. "They were, in a sense, the Mumford and sons of their day."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 50 Biggest Alt-Rock One-Hit Wonders of All Time: Part 2 (40-31)

podcast.title: Era Influence
podcast.body: Mumford & Sons characterized an era of indie rock that was prevalent around 2012-2013, known for its use of banjos and mandolins, and a "melodic, woe-as-me introspective" sound. This era made it challenging for traditional rock bands to gain traction.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Billy Talent In Their Own Words: Part 3

podcast.title: Marcus Mumford's Career Path Change
podcast.body: After attending Captain Kick and the Cowboy Ramblers' performance at The Bosens Locker, Marcus Mumford was so impressed that he dropped out of Edinburgh University, where he was expected to follow his parents into the ministry, and committed to music as his vocation. "Marcus was so impressed by what he heard and saw that he dropped out of university and vowed to make music his vocation."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Marcus Mumford's Family Background
podcast.body: Marcus Mumford's English parents, John (a former "drug-taken hippie" turned ordained minister) and Eleanor (a proponent of faith healing), lived in Orange County, California, where they established a branch of the Vinyard Churches, a Christian evangelical organization, before moving back to London. "His English parents, John, a former drug-taken hippie turned ordained minister, and Eleanor, a proponent of faith healing, were living in Orange County, California at the time, right in the hearts of American punk rock country."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Marcus Mumford's Musical Influences
podcast.body: Growing up, Marcus Mumford was exposed to Bob Dylan's music (especially his "God Love and Era" and the *O Brother, Where Art Thou?* soundtrack) and various jazz. He played in a jazz group as a teenager. "As he grew up, Marcus was exposed to the music of Bob Dylan, especially his God Love and Era, the old brother were at the O Soundtrack, and a variety of jazz."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Multi-Award Winning Status
podcast.body: Mumford & Sons have achieved significant success, becoming a multi-platinum, Grammy-winning, and Brit-winning band. "A multi-platinum, Grammy winning, Brit winning band that plays the banjo."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Name Origin and Meaning
podcast.body: The band evolved from "Marcus Mumford and his Mary Men" to "Mumford & Sons." This name choice, influenced by a trend of bands using "Sons" in their names, was appealing because it evoked the image of a traditional, family-owned general store or antique furniture shop. "So it came to pass that Mumford and his merry men became Mumford & Sons."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Overall Career Success
podcast.body: Beyond their debut, Mumford & Sons have sold well over 10 million albums and accumulated numerous awards and major festival appearances. "Now they've sold well over 10 million albums and have a ton of awards and major festival appearances to their credit."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Pioneering Acoustic Alt Rock
podcast.body: Mumford & Sons achieved significant success with their debut album and single in late 2009, which played a pivotal role in setting the stage for the rise of acoustic-based or acoustic-tinged alt-rock throughout the second decade of the 21st century. Their music demonstrated that folk and bluegrass influences could be successfully introduced to the alt-rock crowd. "Their success, and they had a lot of it, set the stage for a lot of acoustic-based or at least acoustic-ting alt-rock in the second decade of the 21st century."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Streaming Success with Pop-Leaning Rock Sound
podcast.body: Mumford and Sons were among the rock bands that experienced successful streams in the 2010s, with their songs reaching hundreds of millions or even billions of listens. Their music was described as leaning towards the pop end of rock, which helped them thrive amidst the shift to streaming consumption. "There was the luminaires, Lorde, Imagine Dragons, Coldplay, Mumford and Sons. They all had songs that streamed hundreds of millions, and in some cases billions of times through the decade."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of the 2010s Part 1: Rock Struggles Again

podcast.title: Ted Dwane's Musical Education
podcast.body: Ted Dwane is the son of a self-made construction mogul and, in addition to playing the banjo, holds a music school diploma in bass performance. "He also played the banjo, but he actually had a music school diploma in bass performance."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Winston Marshall's Elite Upbringing
podcast.body: Winston Marshall is the son of a highly successful hedge fund manager who managed over 100 million pounds in assets and advised Rupert Murdoch on acquisitions. Despite attending a private school with 30,000 pounds annual tuition, Winston adopted a distinctive "rastaffarian hip-hop gangster" style, complete with dreadlocks. "Winston Marshall, the son of a tremendously successful hedge fund manager that looked after more than 100 million pounds in assets."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: YouTube Record Broken (2009)
xref.body: Lady Gaga previously held a YouTube view record that was surpassed by Mumford & Sons' "Winter Winds" on December 6, 2009. "Winter Winds" achieved 250,000 views in 12 hours, breaking Lady Gaga's record by more than 25%. "And that broke the previous record, said by Lady Gaga, by more than 25%."
